problem: Urban navigation foundation models (e.g. CityWalker) map monocular pixels directly to actions, with depth-scale ambiguity and noisy pseudo-labels, assuming 4D geometry/motion understanding emerges implicitly from large pixel-to-action supervision. Large-scale in-the-wild stereo navigation data is also absent.
motivation: Dynamic, unstructured urban scenes (pedestrians, irregular layouts) demand accurate geometry and motion understanding, but pixel-to-action data is hard to scale. Pretrained vision foundation models (depth, dense tracking) supply this structure explicitly, and stereo gives metric scale, so injecting them should improve data efficiency and accuracy.
key_idea: Feed stereo inputs and explicit mid-level 4D cues (all DINOv2 patch tokens, depth embeddings, CoTracker3 dense tracks via a Tracktention-style track transformer) into a navigation transformer, trained on a newly mined Internet stereo walking dataset (StereoUrban).
insight: Explicit mid-level vision gives strong inductive bias: the ablation shows MAOE dropping from 17.55 (CLS only) to 16.90 (patch tokens), 16.23 (+depth), and 15.77 (+depth+tracking), with depth and tracking complementary. Training-efficiency curves show the model matches/surpasses CityWalker trained on 2000+ hours using ~30 hours (1.5%). Stereo further helps beyond a monocular variant on the stereo benchmark.
method: Image tokenization: DINOv2 retaining all patch tokens (instead of a single CLS token) to keep fine spatial structure
Depth embedding: DepthAnythingV2 depth (monocular) or MonSter++ stereo depth/disparity, encoded by a small CNN and concatenated with the patch tokens

Track transformer (Tracktention-style): CoTracker3 dense tracks; cross-attention pools image tokens into track features, temporal self-attention along each track, then cross-attention writes back to update image tokens

Global attention + target token: sub-goal waypoint and past trajectory are MLP-projected to tokens, jointly processed with image tokens via self-attention; the target token feeds an arrival head and an action head predicting the next N waypoints
Loss: waypoint loss + arrival loss (weight 1.0) + direction loss (weight 10.0)
StereoUrban dataset: Qwen2-VL filters Internet VR180 walking clips for goal-directed forward walking; MAC-VO stereo odometry gives pseudo-action labels; 600 clips, ~60 hours, multiple global cities

setting.backbone: DINOv2 + DepthAnythingV2/MonSter++ + CoTracker3 (pretrained vision modules) with a trained navigation transformer (track transformer, global attention, MLP heads)
setting.training_data: CityWalker monocular data subset (~30 hours, 1.5% of CityWalker's 2000+ h) for the monocular model; StereoUrban (600 clips, ~60 h) plus teleoperated expert stereo data (Jackal, ZED 2i) for fine-tuning
setting.observation: Short window of rectified stereo (or monocular) RGB frames plus past positions and sub-goal waypoint
setting.action_space: Predicted short-horizon waypoints (5 future waypoints over 5 s), converted to velocity commands by a ROS 2 controller
setting.simulator: none (offline real-world data benchmarks; real robot)
setting.privileged: none (at test time; MAC-VO/SLAM used only for label generation)

numbers.extra: fine-tuned on CityWalker teleoperation data; L2 in m, MAOE in degrees
numbers.evidence: Table 1 Monocular Benchmark, StereoWalker rows (Mean and All columns)

numbers.extra: success = within 1 m of target without collision; CityWalker zero-shot gets 50.0 All

numbers_note: Benchmarks are custom offline waypoint-prediction benchmarks (not standard canonical ones); per-scenario columns (Turn, Cross, etc.) omitted for brevity. Training-efficiency results are only in a figure.
results: On the CityWalker benchmark the fine-tuned model achieves best mean MAOE 14.9 and arrival 82.8 vs CityWalker's 15.2 / 81.8; on the stereo benchmark stereo input gives MAOE 2.9 and arrival 94.6 vs CityWalker's 3.7 / 91.2. Real-robot success is 73.8% vs 50.0% for CityWalker, and the model matches CityWalker using 1.5% of its data.
limitations: Weak on Turn scenarios, attributed to data imbalance toward straight segments
Higher inference cost than CityWalker (2.89 GB VRAM, 0.2 s vs 1.68 GB, 0.06 s) and runs remotely on a GPU server
Not explored beyond ground urban robots; data curation pipeline still needs to scale
